title: The Confident Number and the Honest Doubt

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Friday, the fourteenth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three to start. Ukraine set a Russian port on fire, and the price of bread twitched.
[curious] A frontier artificial-intelligence model got given away for free — with a lock on the door for half the West.
And in India, forty million people are paying, by the minute, for someone to tell them it'll be alright.
[curious] Okay, that last one's the whole episode for me. But start with the fire.
Overnight, the eleventh into the twelfth. Ukraine hit Novorossiysk — Russia's main Black Sea naval base, and its biggest grain port. Drones, missiles, uncrewed boats.
Two jobs, one target.
Exactly. Four warships damaged — two frigates, a missile ship, a patrol ship. Two grain terminals stopped work. And Chicago wheat futures jumped about three per cent.
Wait — wheat? Because it's the export gate?
Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter. Hit the port and you've got a hand on the price of bread from Cairo to Lagos.
[thoughtful] And the human cost?
At least three killed, including an eight-year-old. A state of emergency. The water was cut for a time.
So how did the three desks read it? You always say the framing is the story.

It is. Kyiv, through the Western wires, calls it strategically significant — a win against the Black Sea Fleet. Moscow calls it a strike on a civilian port and leads with the child. And Doha follows the wheat downstream — to Africa and the Middle East, who buy the grain and had no part in the war.
Three true things, pointing three ways.
And here's the tell. Kyiv left one thing standing — the oil terminal part-owned by Chevron and ExxonMobil. On an American request, reportedly from Vice-President Vance.
[gasps] They deliberately spared the American oil.
Which tells you it isn't a blockade. It's a message. And the sceptic's line — Russia's already rerouting cargo through the Baltic and Caspian. Terminals get repaired in weeks.
So symbolic, not decisive.
Unless there's a second strike. That's what would change it.
[sighs] Alright. Money block. And I hear the stock market threw a party.
It did. The S and P five hundred closed at a record — seven thousand, seven hundred and ninety-nine. First time ever above seven thousand eight hundred.
On what?
A mild inflation print. July consumer prices up three point four per cent on the year — the second cool one running.
So everyone's happy. Records everywhere.
[deadpan] That's the party upstairs. Go to the basement.
[chuckles] The basement being?
The bond market. Same week, the thirty-year Treasury auction cleared at the dearest financing rate in about twenty-five years. The ten-year, the highest yield since two thousand and seven.
So money is more expensive than it's been in a generation — while stocks make records.

That's the signal. Stocks are pricing relief. The long bond is pricing a hawkish Fed that has no reason to cut, and a pile of government borrowing. When both stocks and long yields rise together, your bonds aren't cushioning your shares.
So for someone holding an all-world tracker and global bonds — diversification's doing less than the record suggests.

Less than it looks. Gold's near a record, about four thousand three hundred and ninety dollars, doing the hedge job. Bitcoin's soft, under sixty-four thousand — a firm dollar and high real yields cap it. The regime's one phrase: higher-for-longer, dollar-bid.
And to be clear — this is explanation, not advice.
Always. We explain the weather. We don't tell you what to wear.
[laughs] Okay. Singapore. There was a big one at home.

The Workers' Party chief, Pritam Singh, was struck off the roll of lawyers on Thursday. The Court of Three Judges — the profession's highest tribunal. Costs of five thousand, eight hundred and eight dollars.
That ends his legal career. Does it end anything else?

That's the whole point — no. Being struck off as a lawyer doesn't vacate a parliamentary seat. He keeps his seat, he keeps the party. It's the automatic consequence of a conviction already litigated last year.
So it's symbolic.
A symbol with limited leverage. No by-election, no vacancy. The risk is atmospheric — an establishment-versus-opposition mood hardening before the National Day Rally on the twenty-third.
And property? You said there was a number that reads two ways.
One number, two stories. A waterfront plot at Berlayar Drive set a record land price — one thousand, five hundred and fifteen dollars a square foot. From a single bidder.
[skeptical] A record set by one guy showing up?

Four to six were expected. One turned up. Read it against a quarterly price index barely positive — up half a per cent, all of it landed homes — and June developer sales at a two-year low. It's a two-speed market: scarce trophy land holding the headline up, the mass market cooling underneath.
So if you own, you're not riding a wave.
You're watching a split. Not advice — but the July sales print, due around the fifteenth, is the tell.
[excited] Right, technology — my corner. The free frontier model.
Alibaba posted the weights of Qwen three-point-eight Max. Two-point-four trillion parameters. Anyone can download it.
That's genuinely huge. So what's the catch — there's always a catch.

The licence. It's a custom, revenue-share licence — not the open Apache terms of before. And one developer read the terms as barring users in the United States, the European Union, Britain and Korea from even downloading it.
[scoffs] An open model you're not allowed to open.

The New Stack called it an API business model wearing an open-source jacket. That reading's disputed and untested — but note, Singapore isn't on the list. A lab here is, on that reading, in the clear.
And the bigger picture — this is the chip-war thing, isn't it?

It is. Washington's now reviewing how Chinese firms rent cutting-edge Nvidia compute offshore. The through-line: export controls slowed the hardware, so the answer was to give the software away as weights.
So can I actually run the two-point-four-trillion thing at home?
[deadpan] No. Not at any size. But the sibling — a dense twenty-seven-billion model — lands this weekend, on a countdown to Friday. That one fits a single card.
A single five-oh-nine-zero.

At eight-bit, about twenty-nine gigabytes — the first single consumer card that runs a model that size at that precision. On two cards, you run it full-precision. But — no spec sheet yet, no benchmarks. It's a countdown, not a review.
So pull it and test it yourself. Don't rebuild the rig on a promise.
That's the discipline.
And gadgets? The Kit?

Two eight-K three-sixty cameras, launched in the same week, cancelling each other out. DJI put the Osmo three-sixty two on stage on Thursday — better on paper. Higher frame rate, replaceable lenses, bigger battery.
So buy the DJI.
[deadpan] With what price? They announced no price. In any market. Not even China. And it may skip American shelves over a regulatory issue.
[laughs] The better camera is the one you can't buy.

The rival, Insta three-sixty's X-six, is on sale now at six hundred and ninety-nine dollars, ninety-nine cents. It's the only one shipping. But we're holding our verdict for the lab bench, around the twenty-sixth.
Wait for the numbers. Got it. [pause] Okay. It's time, isn't it.
[wry] It's time.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every week with this.
[warmly] And it's a good one. Pirate radio. Which, funny enough, has an anniversary this very weekend.

It does. At the midnight turn of the fourteenth into the fifteenth of August, nineteen sixty-seven — fifty-nine years ago — Britain's Marine Broadcasting Offences Act came into force, and a boatload of disc jockeys anchored in international waters legally became criminals.
[excited] Anchored in international waters. Tell me everything.

Last week we followed the shortwave listener. This is the same wire from the other end — the act of transmitting. And here's the whole story in one line: pressing receive is legal everywhere. Pressing transmit is a crime almost everywhere.
So why do people do it?

The romantic engine, everywhere, is a community the licensed dial ignores. In nineteen sixties Britain, it was pop music the BBC wouldn't play. Radio Caroline launched in nineteen sixty-four off the Essex coast — first record, the Beatles, Can't Buy Me Love.
[laughs] Of course it was.
And here's the beautiful part. Caroline still broadcasts today — fully legal now, on the medium-wave, from a ship called the Ross Revenge. That ship is on our cover.
Outlaw ship to licensed heritage broadcaster, same hull. [pause] But it's not all romance, is it.

It isn't. And this is the fact that punctures it. The reason states hunt these stations isn't the music. It's interference. Pirate signals bleed onto safety-of-life bands — there are documented cases of an unlicensed station interfering with an air-traffic control frequency.
[thoughtful] Planes.

Planes. So regulators send direction-finding vans to triangulate a transmitter. In America, the twenty-twenty PIRATE Act pushed the maximum fine, with inflation, to two point four five million dollars.
[gasps] Two and a half million. For a radio station in a bedroom.

They now fine the landlords too. And the community itself is split. There are the log-keepers — meticulous, watch-don't-touch — and the free-radio activists, who see it as a civil right. Some of the most sympathetic stations are in Brooklyn, broadcasting in Haitian Creole to immigrants the commercial dial priced out.
So there the enforcement looks less like protecting a runway and more like policing the poor.
Both are true at once. That's the honest tension. And here's the deflating punchline, Theo, since you love the romance.
[skeptical] Go on.

In twenty twenty-six, a stream reaches more people than any transmitter. Caroline's crime in nineteen sixty-four was that there was no other way to be heard. Today, a Discord and an audio stream reach further, everywhere, legally. The transmitter is now the least effective way to do the thing pirates actually care about.
[sighs] You've just told me the romance is obsolete.
I've told you the itch has a legal scratch. Community low-power licences. Ham radio. A stream. Admire the cathedral — don't light the match.
[warmly] That's a good line. Alright — and you get to pick the next descent. Astronomy, fountain pens, or coral reef aquariums.
Vote on your dashboard. Now — the fast stuff, then the close.
Culture. The movies had a record.
The biggest box-office summer ever — the American domestic total crossed four billion dollars. Driven by a record Spider-Man opening, about three hundred and sixty million, and Nolan's Odyssey.
So cinema's back.
[deadpan] Read the ticket price first. That record leans on record-high ticket prices and premium-format surcharges — nominal dollars, not seats sold. A strong season, not a historic surge.
The asterisk. And on the good-life side — speakers?

Bowers and Wilkins redrew its eight hundred series at sixty — the first full redesign since twenty twenty-one. On sale the ninth of September, from fifteen thousand dollars to sixty-five thousand a pair.
Sixty-five thousand. [exhales] And is it worth it?

The measurement crowd says the room and the placement matter more than the badge, and the resale is soft. The honest note for a buy-once buyer: demo it in your own room before you fall for the top of the range.
Two quick ones for the household. Kids and the body.

The family desk: girls quit sport at exactly the tween years — eleven to thirteen — and reaching puberty predicts dropping the individual sports especially. The fix isn't a pep talk. It's keeping her in a team, where the social scaffolding survives the self-consciousness.
Keep her in the team. And the skincare panic?

The Sephora-kids study is a hundred videos, not a hundred children. The real risk is a narrow band of harsh ingredients. The boring, evidence-backed answer: a cleanser, a moisturiser, and sunscreen. Only about a quarter of those routines used sunscreen.
And fitness — the number I should update?

Protein. The old figure, zero point eight grams per kilo, was set for a sedentary adult. Past forty, when you're losing about a per cent of muscle a year, the target's nearer one to one point two grams per kilo — with two lifting sessions a week. General guidance, not medical advice.
Lift twice, eat the protein. [pause] Okay. Take us down slow. The Undercurrent.

One more for the diary, because the calendar's filling. October in Singapore is a single crowded fortnight — the Formula One weekend adds its first-ever Saturday sprint, and several ticket categories are already sold out.
[excited] A sprint at the night race. That's worth planning a weekend around.
And book the flights for a Japanese autumn — Ghibli Park's adding Porco Rosso's seaplane from November. But the opening to actually book at home is a restaurant: Assaggi, on Neil Road.
Sell me on it.

It's the casual sibling to a one-Michelin-star kitchen — the same chef, a set-menu lunch at fifty-eight dollars. A Michelin kitchen at a lunch price. The food desks are, for once, unanimous. Go on a weekday, before the internet finishes discovering it.
[amused] A weekday lunch. Noted. Alright — take us down slow.

[thoughtful] India. And it arrived, as these things do, in a funding note. An app called Astrotalk — where you pay to speak, live, by the minute, to one of forty-five thousand astrologers — just crossed a one-billion-dollar valuation. India's newest unicorn.
[thoughtful] Astrology. As a billion-dollar business.
Forty million users. A market projected to grow from about a hundred and sixty-three million dollars to one point eight billion by twenty thirty. And follow the money to what it's really buying.
Which is?

Reassurance. Sixty per cent of the questions are about love and relationships. Queries about whether artificial intelligence will take your job rose about half in a year. This is a generation staring down a tightening job market, delayed marriage, urban loneliness.
And there's no-one else to ask.

That's the argument. India has roughly zero point seven five psychiatrists per hundred thousand people, against a benchmark near three. An eighty-five per cent treatment gap. Nearly two hundred million people who need care and mostly don't get it.
[warmly] So the market is building the thing the state never did.

A voice on the line at ten rupees a minute that never puts you on a six-month waitlist. The apps read less like entertainment and more like infrastructure. And the deeper signal — the old idea that a country secularises as it modernises looks simply wrong here. India isn't losing its faith to the smartphone. It's platformising it. Floating a loneliness on the stock exchange.
That's a haunting sentence.

And a precarious business. The regulator is already forcing disclaimers; most users say they doubt the accuracy; and the fastest-growing line is selling remedies — gemstones — to the anxious. Growth built on distress comes with a regulator attached.
[thoughtful] The stars didn't change. The business model did.

And that's the thread of the whole issue. A stock index prints a record while the bond market says the opposite. A land price sets a record from a single bidder. And forty million people pay for a certainty no-one can honestly sell.
So what's the reader supposed to hold onto?
Voltaire, on the contents page. Doubt is not a pleasant condition — but certainty is absurd. Prefer the honest doubt to the confident number.
[warmly] Trust the antenna, not the volume.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
